title: Birth outcomes and prenatal exposure to ozone, carbon monoxide, and particulate matter: results from the Children's Health Study.
ehr_evidence: Birth certificate information for California-born children who participated in the CHS was obtained by computerized linkage of participants with the California Department of Health Services Birth Statistical Master Files and Birth Cohort Files.
summary: In a population-based cohort of 3,901 term infants born in California (1975-1987) participating in the Children's Health Study, prenatal exposure to ambient air pollutants (ozone, carbon monoxide, PM10, NO2) was associated with reduced birth weight and increased risk of IUGR and LBW.
key_findings: A 12-ppb increase in 24-hr ozone averaged over the entire pregnancy was associated with 47.2 g lower birth weight (95% CI, 27.4-67.0 g), most robust for second- and third-trimester exposures.
A 1.4-ppm difference in first-trimester carbon monoxide exposure was associated with 21.7 g lower birth weight (95% CI, 1.1-42.3 g) and a 20% increased risk of IUGR (95% CI, 1.0-1.4).
First-trimester CO and third-trimester O3 exposures were associated with a 20% increased risk of IUGR.
A 20-µg/m3 difference in PM10 during the third trimester was associated with 21.7 g lower birth weight (95% CI, 1.1-42.2 g), but this was reduced and no longer significant after adjusting for O3.
Third-trimester O3 exposure was associated with a 40% increased risk of LBW (95% CI, 1.0-1.9), though estimates had substantial uncertainty due to the small number of LBW newborns.
NO2 was not significantly associated with birth weight.
Exposures to PM10, NO2, and CO averaged over the entire pregnancy were not significantly associated with birth weight.
captured_features: maternal residence ZIP code at birth
population: 3,901 term infants (gestational age 37-44 weeks) born in California 1975-1987, participants in the population-based Children's Health Study across 12 southern California communities
exposure_domain: air pollution (ozone, carbon monoxide, particulate matter PM10, nitrogen dioxide)
limitations: Air pollution exposure was assigned based on the ZIP code centroid of maternal residence at childbirth, which may not reflect actual exposure during the entire pregnancy, and residential address most often reflects the last trimester.
Lacked information on maternal employment location and commuting patterns, contributing to non-differential exposure misclassification.
No direct measures of maternal indoor and occupational pollutant exposures.
Small number of LBW newborns (<2% prevalence) led to substantial uncertainty in LBW estimates.
Gestational age was based on maternal recall of last menstrual period, which may be less accurate.
Measurement error in pollutant estimates, particularly in two-pollutant models, may attenuate effect estimates.
